The French Open, officially known as Roland-Garros. Held each May at the Stade Roland-Garros in Paris, it is played on red clay courts and stands as the second Grand Slam tournament of the calendar year. The tournament is renowned as the most physically demanding major championship, where clay court specialists and tactical players have historically flourished.

The tournament was named after Roland-Garros, a French aviator and fighter pilot from the First World War. The facility was renamed in his honor in nineteen twenty six. The tournament itself was first held in eighteen ninety one as a French national championship, but it did not open to international competitors until nineteen twenty five, transforming it into a truly global event.

The red clay surface profoundly shapes the tournament's character and determines which champion profiles emerge. The clay significantly slows the ball and extends rallies, heavily favoring players with strong baseline games and exceptional footwork. This creates a different champion profile than grass courts or hard courts, rewarding endurance and tactical tennis rather than pure power.

Rafael Nadal has won the tournament a record tying fourteen times, establishing himself as the greatest clay court player of all time. His dominance on clay at Roland-Garros represents an unmatched achievement in tennis history. Chris Evert won seven French Open singles titles and was known as the Queen of Clay, dominating the tournament throughout the nineteen seventies and nineteen eighties. Roger Federer won the French Open once in two thousand nine, and this victory completed his career Grand Slam, winning all four major championships. He achieved this at the age of twenty seven. Serena Williams won three French Open singles titles during her dominance of women's tennis. Björn Borg won the French Open six times and was one of the few players to excel on both clay and grass courts.

The tournament is associated with slower matches and longer rallies than other majors, testing endurance and tactical tennis more profoundly than any other Grand Slam.
